new_statements.quote: [7.1, p.22] Greater intensity, greater length and a tenser vocoid segment evidence stress. Using this basis, stress is not contrastive in the vast majority of cases. In two-syllable words it generally falls on the second syllable, leaving the first, unstressed syllable with a much shorter and quieter more neutral vowel. [...] In the vast majority of three-syllable words it is easier to place the stress, and it can occur on any of the three syllables. [2.3, p.3] In words of three or more syllables the stress is not predictable, but nor is it contrastive. Pitch is phonemically contrastive [...] Here the pitch contrast is on the final stressed syllable if the word has more than one syllable, and consists of a difference between a relatively flat contour and a falling contour.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress (intensity, length, fuller vowel) is largely non-contrastive: disyllables are generally stressed on the second = final syllable (with counterexamples and some evenly stressed words); in words of three or more syllables the stressed syllable is lexically unpredictable but carries no contrast; the phonemic prosodic contrast is a flat (high) vs falling pitch contour realised on the stressed syllable (word-level tone / pitch-accent-like). NB the same team's 1998 Pacific Linguistics grammar sketch instead states regular PENULTIMATE stress with a few final-stressed lexical exceptions; the 1992 OPD, the 2000 phonology, King 2000 and Cahill 2011 all agree on second-syllable prominence in disyllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. Compounds share a single primary stress (Bennett & Bennett 1998:153).
new_statements.exceptions: 'Several' disyllables with even prominence on both syllables (e.g. sarum 'clam shell'); 'a very few' stress-only minimal pairs (wuduud 'he is swimming' vs wuduud 'dolphin'; wiyuw 'his nose/mountain' vs wiyuw 'rat'); King 2000 orthography paper: 'a significant number of counterexamples' to 2nd-syllable stress in disyllables; Cahill 2011: gaogao 'crow' has the contrastive syllable first. Bennett & Bennett 1998:152 (contradicting): penultimate stress with 'very few exceptions... stressed on the ultimate syllable'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statements based on citation forms (orthographic words, Yamai dialect); 1998 grammar defines words as 'phonological stress groups' of 1-6 syllables; King & Bennett 2000 sec.8.1 separately describes phrase-level tonic syllable (often phrase-initial) and stress-timed rhythm. Analysis explicitly labelled preliminary/draft ('enough counterexamples to warrant further investigation').
new_statements.identity_note: All Bennett/King work describes the Yamai village ('samang') dialect of Awad Bing (awad1244; the OPD is headed 'Awad Bing [Yamai dialect]'). Simons & Simons 1977 describes the Biliau village communalect of the same language under the older name Biliau. No sub-glottocodes exist for these dialects.

sources.note: Sec.2.3 p.152: 'Words in Awad Bing are phonological stress groups consisting of from one to six syllables. Stress is usually predictable, occurring on the penultimate syllable of each word, with very few exceptions which do not appear to form a predictable class, but are stressed on the ultimate syllable providing a contrast to the penultimate stress.' Also p.153: compound nouns share one primary stress; p.204: attributive NPs have stress on each word. CONTRADICTS the 2000 phonology and the authors' own 1992 OPD on disyllables.

sources.citation: King, Phil. 2000. Awad Bing Orthography. Working paper, SIL PNG, 20 Oct 2000, 9 pp. SIL archives 56763.
sources.note: Sec.2.4 pp.3-4: in disyllables stress generally on the 2nd syllable, with a significant number of counterexamples; a small number of stress-only minimal pairs (wuduud); for 3+ syllables stress not contrastive and can fall on any syllable; pitch (flat vs falling) and length function together.

sources.citation: Bennett, Douglas & Jeanette Bennett. 1992 (data checked Aug 1992; printed 2004). Awad Bing [Yamai dialect] Organised Phonology Data. SIL PNG, 6 pp. SIL archives 42461.
sources.note: p.4 'Suprasegmentals': 'Most two syllable words have a stressed second syllable. In words of three or more syllables there is more variation. Stress is phonemic in some cases but the functional load is small. There are phonemic pitch contrasts between vowel segments with a high flat tone and those with a falling tone. Pitch information is only carried phonemically on stressed syllables.'

sources.citation: Cahill, Michael. 2011. Tonal diversity in languages of Papua New Guinea. SIL Electronic Working Papers 2011-008, 23 pp.

sources.note: Sec.4 pp.15-17 (first-hand but 'preliminary' data): Awad Bing has contrastive High vs Falling tone on only one syllable per word; on disyllables the contrastive syllable is consistently the second (exception gaogao 'crow'); on trisyllabic or longer words its location is unpredictable; p.19-20 characterises it as combining pitch-accent and tonal properties. No independent stress rule.
